items.stem: Who proposed the idea of continental drift, and what did he name the ancient supercontinent?

options.text: Isaac Newton; Gondwana
Alfred Wegener; Pangaea
Charles Darwin; Laurasia
Alfred Wegener; Atlantis

items.explanation: In 1912, the German scientist Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift and named the supercontinent Pangaea, meaning all land.

items.stem: Wegener found fossils of the same plant, Glossopteris, on continents now separated by wide oceans. Why is this evidence that the continents were once joined?

options.text: The seeds were too heavy to drift across an ocean and the animals could not swim that far
Glossopteris still grows on every continent today
Fossils can float across oceans on currents
The plant only grew in freezing climates

items.explanation: Glossopteris seeds could not survive a long ocean drift, and the small land animals found with it could not swim across oceans. The simplest explanation is that the land was once connected.

items.stem: The lithosphere is broken into large slabs that float on the asthenosphere. What are these slabs called?

options.text: Convection cells
Rift valleys
Tectonic plates
Continental shelves

items.explanation: The rigid lithosphere is cracked into tectonic plates that slowly move over the soft, flowing asthenosphere.

items.stem: Wegener could not explain what moved the continents. What actually provides the force that moves the plates?

options.text: The pull of ocean tides
The spinning of the inner core
Wind and weather at the surface
Convection currents in the mantle

items.explanation: Heat inside Earth drives convection currents in the mantle. The flowing mantle rock drags the plates, which is the force Wegener was missing.

items.stem: At a divergent boundary two plates move apart. What happens in the gap between them?

options.text: Rising magma fills the gap and cools into new crust
One plate sinks beneath the other
The plates grind past each other
A deep ocean trench forms

items.explanation: As the plates separate, magma rises to fill the gap and cools into new crust. Under the ocean this is seafloor spreading at a mid-ocean ridge.

items.stem: The seafloor of the Atlantic is youngest at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and older farther away. Which process best explains this?

options.text: Subduction pulling the crust down
Seafloor spreading at a divergent boundary
A transform fault sliding sideways
Weathering of the ocean floor

items.explanation: New crust forms at the ridge and moves outward, so the seafloor is youngest at the ridge and gets older with distance. This is seafloor spreading.

items.stem: Two oceanic plates collide and the more dense one sinks beneath the other. What is this process called, and what does it tend to build?

options.text: Spreading, building a rift valley
Erosion, building canyons
Subduction, building volcanoes and island arcs
Drifting, building flat plains

items.explanation: When one plate sinks beneath another it is called subduction. The sinking plate melts and feeds volcanoes, forming features like the Japanese island arc.

items.stem: The Himalayas formed where two continental plates of similar density collided. Why did they crumple upward instead of one plate sinking?

options.text: Continental crust is too dense to rise
One of the plates melted completely
The boundary is actually a transform boundary
Neither plate is dense enough to sink, so they push each other up

items.explanation: Continental crust is light and does not subduct easily. When two continental plates meet, neither sinks, so the crust folds and pushes upward into tall mountains like the Himalayas.

items.stem: The San Andreas Fault is a place where two plates slide past each other. What kind of boundary is this, and what is it known for?

options.text: A transform boundary known for earthquakes
A divergent boundary known for new seafloor
A convergent boundary known for volcanoes
A boundary known for building island arcs

items.explanation: Plates sliding past each other form a transform boundary. They catch and slip, releasing energy as earthquakes, like those along the San Andreas Fault.

items.stem: Why do earthquakes and volcanoes occur in narrow belts around Earth rather than randomly?

options.text: They follow ocean currents around the globe
They line up along the edges of the tectonic plates
They appear wherever the crust is thickest
They are spread evenly but only reported in cities

items.explanation: Almost all earthquakes and volcanoes happen at plate boundaries, where plates pull apart, collide, or slide past. The belts on the map trace those boundaries.
